<div class="markdown"><p>Chapter 2 started from one generator, the adjacent swap, and derived a quotient: every ordering of the same flips collapses to one head count. We chose that generator by hand. This chapter treats the choice as an inference problem. Given a small library of candidate generators, which one should a learner use for a given task?</p><p>Each candidate generator groups sequences into orbits, and we label each orbit by a <em>canonical form</em>: one fixed member chosen to stand for the whole orbit. A candidate is useful for a task when the task's answer is constant on each orbit, because a decoder can then read the answer from the canonical form. Among the candidates that pass this test, we prefer the one with the fewest orbits, because its decoder has fewer cases to handle.</p><p>Choosing what to ignore is only half the story. The chapter ends by asking how to describe the chosen quotient so that the task becomes simple to compute. A description in which the task needs only a few cheap, ideally linear, operations is what the paper calls a <em>normal form</em>.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="The-model-and-the-two-tasks">The model and the two tasks</h2><p>We reuse the coin model from Chapter 1 and the two tasks from Chapter 2: the posterior probability that the coin is fair, and the longest run of heads.</p></div>

```julia
coin_flip(i, ω) =
    (i ~ Bernoulli(is_fair_coin(ω) ? fair_weight : trick_weight))(ω)
```

```julia
flip_sequence(n) = Variable(ω -> [coin_flip(i, ω) for i in 1:n])
```

```julia
show_sequence(sequence) = join(ifelse.(sequence, "H", "T"))
```

```julia
function is_fair_posterior(sequence)
    likelihood(weight) = prod(flip ? weight : 1 - weight for flip in sequence)
    fair_mass = is_fair_prior * likelihood(fair_weight)
    trick_mass = (1 - is_fair_prior) * likelihood(trick_weight)
    fair_mass / (fair_mass + trick_mass)
end
```

```julia
function longest_head_run(sequence)
    longest = 0
    current = 0
    for s in sequence
        current = s ? current + 1 : 0
        longest = max(longest, current)
    end
    longest
end
```

```julia
function swap_adjacent(sequence, i)
    swapped = copy(sequence)
    swapped[i], swapped[i + 1] = swapped[i + 1], swapped[i]
    swapped
end
```

```julia
all_boolean_sequences(n) = [
    [isone((mask >> i) & 1) for i in 0:n-1]
    for mask in 0:(2^n - 1)
]
```

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="A-library-of-candidate-generators">A library of candidate generators</h2><p>Each candidate below returns the <em>neighbours</em> of a sequence: the sequences reachable by one application of one of its generators.</p><ul><li><p><code>identity</code> has no generators, so every sequence is its own orbit.</p></li><li><p><code>reversal</code> reverses the whole sequence.</p></li><li><p><code>rotation</code> moves the last flip to the front, a cyclic shift.</p></li><li><p><code>permutation</code> uses the adjacent swaps from Chapter 2, which generate every reordering.</p></li></ul></div>

```julia
generator_library = [
    :identity    => sequence -> Vector{Bool}[],
    :reversal    => sequence -> [reverse(sequence)],
    :rotation    => sequence -> [circshift(sequence, 1)],
    :permutation => sequence -> [swap_adjacent(sequence, i) for i in 1:length(sequence)-1],
]
```

```text
4-element Vector{Pair{Symbol, Function}}:

    :reversal => Main.var"#9#14"{typeof(reverse)}(reverse)
    :rotation => Main.var"#10#15"{typeof(circshift)}(circshift)
 :permutation => Main.var"#11#16"{typeof(swap_adjacent), typeof(-), Colon, typeof(length)}(Main.var"workspace#3".swap_adjacent, -, Colon(), length)
```
{: .notebook-output}

<div class="markdown"><p><code>orbit</code> generalises <code>permutation_orbit</code> from Chapter 2. It takes any neighbour function, repeatedly applies it, and collects every sequence it reaches. The canonical form is the alphabetically first member of the orbit, writing <code>H</code> before <code>T</code>. Any fixed choice of representative would work; what matters is that every member of an orbit maps to the same one.</p></div>

```julia
function orbit(neighbours, sequence)
    seen = Set([sequence])
    frontier = [sequence]
    while !isempty(frontier)
        current = popfirst!(frontier)
        for candidate in neighbours(current)
            if candidate ∉ seen
                push!(seen, candidate)
                push!(frontier, candidate)
            end
        end
    end
    sort(collect(seen), by = show_sequence)
end
```

```julia
canonical_form(neighbours, sequence) = first(orbit(neighbours, sequence))
```

```julia

```

```julia
    (generator = name,
     orbit = show_sequence.(orbit(neighbours, seed_sequence)),
     canonical_form = show_sequence(canonical_form(neighbours, seed_sequence)))
    for (name, neighbours) in generator_library
]
```

<div class="markdown"><p>For <code>HHTH</code>, <code>identity</code> leaves the sequence alone and <code>reversal</code> pairs it with <code>HTHH</code>. <code>rotation</code> and <code>permutation</code> both reach all four sequences with three heads, so they share the canonical form <code>HHHT</code>.</p><p>The two differ on other seeds. Try <code>[true, true, false, false]</code> and then <code>[true, false, true, false]</code>. Permutation puts <code>HHTT</code> and <code>HTHT</code> in the same orbit; rotation keeps them apart, because no cyclic shift turns one into the other.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="How-coarse-is-each-quotient?">How coarse is each quotient?</h2><p>The quotient of a candidate is its set of orbits. The next cells group every sequence of a given length by its canonical form and count the groups.</p></div>

```julia
sequence_length = 4
```

```text
4
```
{: .notebook-output}

```julia
function quotient_classes(neighbours, n)
    classes = Dict{Vector{Bool}, Vector{Vector{Bool}}}()
    for sequence in all_boolean_sequences(n)
        push!(get!(classes, canonical_form(neighbours, sequence), Vector{Bool}[]), sequence)
    end
    classes
end
```

```julia
class_count(neighbours, n) = length(quotient_classes(neighbours, n))
```

```julia
[(generator = name, classes = class_count(neighbours, sequence_length))
 for (name, neighbours) in generator_library]
```

```text
4-element Vector{@NamedTuple{generator::Symbol, classes::Int64}}:
 (generator = :identity, classes = 16)
 (generator = :reversal, classes = 10)
 (generator = :rotation, classes = 6)
 (generator = :permutation, classes = 5)
```
{: .notebook-output}

<div class="markdown"><p>For four flips, you should see 16, 10, 6 and 5 classes for each generator, respectively. <code>identity</code> keeps all 16 sequences apart. <code>reversal</code> pairs each sequence with its mirror image and leaves the four palindromes alone, giving 4 + 12/2 = 10. <code>rotation</code> gives 6 classes, and <code>permutation</code> gives the five head counts from Chapter 2.</p><p>Fewer classes means a smaller table for the decoder. Try <code>sequence_length = 5</code> and predict the counts first: 32 sequences, 8 of them palindromes.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="Task-sufficiency">Task sufficiency</h2><p>A quotient is <em>sufficient</em> for a task <span class="tex">\(T\)</span> when <span class="tex">\(T\)</span> is constant on every class. Then a decoder <span class="tex">\(D\)</span> exists with <span class="tex">\(T = D\circ q\)</span>, where <span class="tex">\(q\)</span> maps a sequence to its canonical form, exactly as in Chapters 1 and 2.</p><p>The fair-coin posterior returns floating-point numbers. Two orderings of the same flips can give values that differ in the last digit, so <code>same_answer</code> compares floats approximately.</p></div>

```julia
same_answer(a, b) = a isa AbstractFloat ? isapprox(a, b) : a == b
```

```julia
function is_task_sufficient(neighbours, task, n)
    for class in values(quotient_classes(neighbours, n))
        reference = task(first(class))
        for s in class
            same_answer(task(s), reference) || return false
        end
    end
    true
end
```

```julia
sufficiency_table = [
    (generator = name,
     classes = class_count(neighbours, sequence_length),
     fair_posterior = is_task_sufficient(neighbours, is_fair_posterior, sequence_length),
     longest_head_run = is_task_sufficient(neighbours, longest_head_run, sequence_length))
    for (name, neighbours) in generator_library
]
```

```text
4-element Vector{@NamedTuple{generator::Symbol, classes::Int64, fair_posterior::Bool, longest_head_run::Bool}}:
 (generator = :identity, classes = 16, fair_posterior = 1, longest_head_run = 1)
 (generator = :reversal, classes = 10, fair_posterior = 1, longest_head_run = 1)
 (generator = :rotation, classes = 6, fair_posterior = 1, longest_head_run = 0)
 (generator = :permutation, classes = 5, fair_posterior = 1, longest_head_run = 0)
```
{: .notebook-output}

<div class="markdown"><p>Every candidate preserves the fair-coin posterior, because each one only reorders flips and the posterior depends only on the head count. Only <code>identity</code> and <code>reversal</code> preserve the longest head run. <code>rotation</code> fails because it can join two runs: it turns <code>HHTH</code> into <code>HHHT</code>, changing the longest run from 2 to 3.</p><p>Reading down each task column, the coarsest sufficient quotient is <code>permutation</code> for the posterior and <code>reversal</code> for the longest run.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="Inferring-the-quotient-from-examples">Inferring the quotient from examples</h2><p>So far we checked sufficiency against every sequence, using the task function itself. A learner usually sees only a few examples: sequences paired with their answers. It has to infer a quotient from those.</p><p>A candidate is <em>consistent</em> with the examples when no two examples share a canonical form but have different answers. If two examples do, no decoder of that quotient can reproduce both answers.</p></div>

```julia
function is_consistent(neighbours, examples)
    answers = Dict{Vector{Bool}, Any}()
    for (sequence, answer) in examples
        key = canonical_form(neighbours, sequence)
        if haskey(answers, key)
            same_answer(answers[key], answer) || return false
        else
            answers[key] = answer
        end
    end
    true
end
```

<div class="markdown"><h3 id="A-simplicity-prior">A simplicity prior</h3><p>The prior prefers candidates with fewer classes. Each candidate gets weight <span class="tex">\(c^{-\lambda}\)</span>, where <span class="tex">\(c\)</span> is its number of classes and <span class="tex">\(\lambda\)</span> is <code>simplicity_strength</code>. Setting it to 0 gives a uniform prior.</p><p>This preference is a modelling choice for this example. What we care about is how costly the task is to compute in each representation; the number of classes is one simple stand-in for that cost. The prior is a cost on representations written as a probability.</p></div>

```julia
simplicity_strength = 1.0
```

```text
1.0
```
{: .notebook-output}

```julia
prior = let
    weights = [class_count(neighbours, sequence_length)^(-simplicity_strength)
               for (_, neighbours) in generator_library]
    weights / sum(weights)
end
```

<div class="markdown"><p>The model draws one candidate from this prior. <code>quotient_posterior</code> conditions that draw on consistency with the examples, so it keeps only candidates whose quotient could explain them.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><p>Because consistency is fixed once the candidate is chosen, the posterior is the prior restricted to the consistent candidates and renormalised. <code>exact_posterior</code> computes that directly so we can compare it with the samples.</p></div>

```julia
function exact_posterior(examples)
    weights = [p * is_consistent(neighbours, examples)
               for ((_, neighbours), p) in zip(generator_library, prior)]
    weights / sum(weights)
end
```

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="Which-cost?">Which cost?</h2><p>The simplicity prior counted classes: the number of cases a decoder has to handle. Class count is one type of cost. Another is the work needed to compute the canonical form of a new sequence. <code>canonical_form</code> enumerates the whole orbit, so its cost grows with orbit size.</p></div>

```julia
mean_orbit_size(neighbours, n) =
    mean(length(orbit(neighbours, s)) for s in all_boolean_sequences(n))
```

```julia
[(generator = name,
  classes = class_count(neighbours, sequence_length),
  mean_orbit_size = mean_orbit_size(neighbours, sequence_length))
 for (name, neighbours) in generator_library]
```

```text
4-element Vector{@NamedTuple{generator::Symbol, classes::Int64, mean_orbit_size::Float64}}:
 (generator = :identity, classes = 16, mean_orbit_size = 1.0)
 (generator = :reversal, classes = 10, mean_orbit_size = 1.75)
 (generator = :rotation, classes = 6, mean_orbit_size = 3.375)
 (generator = :permutation, classes = 5, mean_orbit_size = 4.375)
```
{: .notebook-output}

<div class="markdown"><p>The two costs rank the candidates in opposite orders. <code>permutation</code> has the fewest classes but the largest orbits: a sequence with <span class="tex">\(k\)</span> heads has <span class="tex">\(\binom{n}{k}\)</span> orderings to enumerate. Try <code>sequence_length = 8</code> and compare.</p><p>Chapter 1 reached the same permutation class far more cheaply. Counting heads takes one pass over the sequence and never builds the orbit. The quotient is the same; only the way of describing it differs. Which representation counts as simplest therefore depends on what you measure, and on which operations the machine doing the computing makes cheap.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="From-a-quotient-to-a-normal-form">From a quotient to a normal form</h2><p>For the fair-coin task we settled on the permutation quotient. The canonical forms <code>HHHT</code>, <code>HHTT</code> and so on label its classes, but they do not make the task easier to compute. The head count from Chapter 1 labels the same classes.</p></div>

```julia
count_coordinate(sequence) = 
    (flips = length(sequence), heads = count(identity, sequence))
```

```julia
permutation_neighbours = Dict(generator_library)[:permutation]
```

```julia
(same_number_of_classes =
     length(unique(count_coordinate.(all_boolean_sequences(sequence_length)))) ==
     class_count(permutation_neighbours, sequence_length),
 one_count_per_class =
     all(length(unique(count_coordinate.(class))) == 1
         for class in values(quotient_classes(permutation_neighbours, sequence_length))))
```

```text
(same_number_of_classes = true, one_count_per_class = true)
```
{: .notebook-output}

<div class="markdown"><p>Both checks should be <code>true</code>: the count and the canonical form describe the same quotient. The descriptions differ in what they make easy.</p><p>As data arrive, the fair-coin task has to track one transformation: observing another flip. For a sequence, observing a flip lengthens a list. In count coordinates it adds <code>(1, 1)</code> for a head or <code>(1, 0)</code> for a tail. <code>append_flip</code> performs this update, and the next cell checks that updating the count gives the same result as counting the longer sequence.</p></div>

```julia
append_flip(coordinate, flip) = 
    (flips = coordinate.flips + 1, heads = coordinate.heads + flip)
```

```julia
all(count_coordinate(vcat(s, flip)) == append_flip(count_coordinate(s), flip)
    for s in all_boolean_sequences(sequence_length) for flip in (true, false))
```

```text
true
```
{: .notebook-output}

<div class="markdown"><p>The posterior is not a linear function of the count, but its <em>log odds</em> is. Each head multiplies the odds that the coin is fair by the same factor, and each tail by another. Taking logarithms turns those products into sums, so every head moves the evidence by a fixed step and every tail by another fixed step.</p></div>

```julia
head_step = log(fair_weight / trick_weight)
```

```text
-0.5306282510621704
```
{: .notebook-output}

```julia
tail_step = log((1 - fair_weight) / (1 - trick_weight))
```

```text
1.203972804325936
```
{: .notebook-output}

```julia
prior_log_odds = log(is_fair_prior / (1 - is_fair_prior))
```

```text
0.0
```
{: .notebook-output}

```julia
fair_log_odds(coordinate) = prior_log_odds + coordinate.heads * head_step +
    (coordinate.flips - coordinate.heads) * tail_step
```

```julia
from_log_odds(z) = 1 / (1 + exp(-z))
```

```julia
all(from_log_odds(fair_log_odds(count_coordinate(s))) ≈ is_fair_posterior(s)
    for s in all_boolean_sequences(sequence_length))
```

```text
true
```
{: .notebook-output}

```julia
[(heads = k,
  log_odds = fair_log_odds((flips = sequence_length, heads = k)),
  fair_posterior = 
  from_log_odds(fair_log_odds((flips = sequence_length, heads = k))))
 for k in 0:sequence_length]
```

<div class="markdown"><p>At the starting settings, each head moves the log odds by about −0.53, towards the trick coin, and each tail by about +1.20, towards the fair coin. The posterior column changes unevenly; the log-odds column changes in equal steps.</p><p>The log odds is a <em>usable axis</em>. Deciding "fair or trick?" means checking its sign, comparing two sequences means comparing two numbers, and observing another flip means adding a step. The canonical forms supported none of these operations directly.</p><p>Two moves produced this description. Quotienting removed the order of the flips, and re-describing the quotient turned the evidence into a sum. A representation in which the task needs only a few cheap, linear operations like these is what the paper calls a normal form. Try changing <code>trick_weight</code> and predict how the two steps change before running the cells.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="What-the-library-leaves-out">What the library leaves out</h2><p>The learner here selects from four candidates that we supplied and cannot invent a fifth generator. Nor did it find the count coordinate or the log-odds axis: we supplied those in the last section. If no candidate were sufficient and cheap, the posterior would still have to choose among them.</p><p>Chapter 4 changes the task partway through and asks how a learner can tell that its representation has stopped working. Constructing new generators and axes is the step that a fixed library cannot take.</p><h2 id="Discussion">Discussion</h2><p>Add a candidate <code>:complement =&gt; sequence -&gt; [.!sequence]</code> that swaps heads and tails. Before running the sufficiency table, predict which tasks it preserves. Would your answer change if <code>trick_weight</code> were 0.5?</p><p>The longest-run task settled on the reversal quotient. Can you find a description of it in which the longest run is cheap to read off?</p><p>With <code>simplicity_strength = 0</code> and complete evidence, the longest-run posterior splits evenly between <code>identity</code> and <code>reversal</code>. What kind of evidence, if any, could favour <code>reversal</code> without a simplicity prior? Consider a learner that must answer questions about sequences it has never seen.</p></div>
